title: Extend the high value council tax surcharge to homes over £1.5m
headline: A £1.5m band, assumed to raise what the £2m band does: £0.4bn.
description: Budget 2025 introduced an annual surcharge on owners of homes in England valued over £2 million from April 2028, costed at £400 million in 2028-29 rising to £435 million. This card adds a lower band from £1.5 million and assumes it raises exactly what the Treasury costed for the £2 million bands, year by year, set-up costs included. That is an assumption, not a costing: nobody has published how many homes sit between £1.5 million and £2 million or what they would be charged.

baselinePolicy.text: A surcharge on owners of residential properties valued over £2 million in England from 1 April 2028, based on a Valuation Office revaluation at 2026 values, on an estimated 165,000 properties in 2028-29; costed at −£60m, −£120m and −£155m of set-up cost in 2025-26 to 2027-28, then £400m, £430m and £435m (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 54).
alreadyIncludes: The £2 million surcharge itself, with the Treasury's allowance for price capitalisation, bunching below the thresholds, appeals, non-payment and a support scheme (Budget 2025 policy costings, pages 51-52).

lines.title: High Value Council Tax Surcharge: Introduce a surcharge on owners of residential properties valued over £2m in England from 1 April 2028

rawSource.note: Repeat: the Treasury's certified costing of the £2 million surcharge, taken as the yield of a further band from £1.5 million, year by year, set-up costs included. Positive scorecard values reduce borrowing; here receipts positive means more revenue. Effects before the start year are not applied.

caveats: Equal yield is our assumption. The Treasury's costing rests on about 165,000 homes over £2 million with banded charges; there are more homes between £1.5 million and £2 million, but a lower band would carry a lower charge, and nobody has published either number. The real figure could be well above or below.
England only, as the surcharge itself is; council tax is devolved elsewhere. The surcharge is scored as an Exchequer receipt, not council revenue.
The set-up costs in 2027-28 are kept: a new band needs valuing too. The Treasury's costing is on the OBR November 2025 forecast, not the March 2026 baseline used here.

considerations.text: The Treasury assumes the surcharge is fully capitalised into prices over three years and that buyers bunch below each threshold; it also allows for appeals, non-payment and a support scheme for owners who cannot pay. A lower threshold catches more homes, more of them owned by people with high housing wealth and modest incomes, so those allowances would bite harder.

Owners of homes worth £1.5 million to £2 million in England, concentrated in London and the South East. The Treasury's own tax base for the £2 million surcharge is 165,000 properties; the Wealth and Assets Survey is used to judge how many could not pay.
